Mission 1

Mission 1: How did poems sung in Tamil, Marathi and Hindi let outcastes and women reach God directly?

Make a guess: How did poems sung in Tamil, Marathi and Hindi let outcastes and women reach God directly?

Mission 1

Bhakti marga: the way of loving devotion

  • Bhakti (from bhaj, "to share in", "to worship"): loving, personal devotion to God.
  • Bhakti marga: the way of devotion, one of the paths to moksha.
  • God is approached as saguna, with qualities: Vishnu (often as Krishna or Rama), Shiva, or the Goddess.
  • The devotee relates to God as servant, friend, parent, child or beloved.
  • The heart of it: love and surrender; liberation through God's grace.
  • Liberation is often seen as eternal loving closeness to God, not loss of self.
Mission 1Read the source

Offered with love, open to all

> "Whate'er thou doest, Prince! / Eating or sacrificing, giving gifts, / Praying or fasting, let it all be done / For Me, as Mine. So shalt thou free thyself / From Karmabandh, the chain which holdeth men / To good and evil issue" (Bhagavad Gita 9:27–28, Arnold)

> "… whoso will turn to Me, / Though they be born from the very womb of Sin, / Woman or man; sprung of the Vaisya caste / Or lowly disregarded Sudra,--all / Plant foot upon the highest path" (Bhagavad Gita 9:32, Arnold)

Q1 According to 9:27–28, how does devotion free a person from karma?

Show answer

By doing every action as an offering to God, not for oneself.

Q2 Who can reach "the highest path" in 9:32?

Show answer

Anyone who turns to God: women and men, of any birth.

Mission 1

Origins: the Tamil saints

  • The movement began in South India, in Tamil, c. 6th–9th centuries CE.
  • Alvars: 12 Vaishnava poet-saints devoted to Vishnu (e.g. Nammalvar; Andal, a woman). Their hymns were gathered as the Four Thousand Divine Hymns.
  • Nayanars: 63 Shaiva saints devoted to Shiva (e.g. Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar; Karaikkal Ammaiyar, a woman). Their hymns form the Tevaram.
  • They sang in Tamil, not Sanskrit, travelling from temple to temple.
  • Background: the Gita's teaching on devotion; temple worship growing; competition with Jain and Buddhist communities in South India.
Mission 1

The movement spreads north

  • Ramanuja (trad. 1017–1137): gives bhakti a philosophical basis.
  • Karnataka, 12th century: Basava and the Lingayats (Shaiva); Akka Mahadevi.
  • Maharashtra: Jnaneshvar (13th century), Namdev, Chokhamela (a Mahar, "untouchable"), Tukaram (17th century): devotees of Vithoba at Pandharpur.
  • North India, 15th–17th centuries: Kabir; Ravidas (a leatherworker); Mirabai (a Rajput princess devoted to Krishna); Surdas; Tulsidas (Ramcharitmanas, Rama's story in Hindi).
  • Bengal: Chaitanya (1486–1534): ecstatic chanting of Krishna's names (kirtan), later the root of ISKCON.
  • Common features: local languages, song, saints from every caste, and women.
Quick check
?Which statement about the Alvars and Nayanars is accurate?
Mission 1

Vaishnava bhakti

  • Loving devotion to Vishnu and his avatars, especially Krishna and Rama.
  • Krishna as child, cowherd and lover; the love of the gopis (cowherd women) in the Bhagavata Purana, and of Radha in later poetry such as Jayadeva's Gita Govinda (12th century), as the model of the soul's longing for God.
  • Rama as the ideal king and the object of devotion (Tulsidas; Hanuman as the perfect devotee).
  • Key ideas: prapatti (surrender) and God's grace.
  • Today: ISKCON, Swaminarayan and many other movements.
Mission 1

Shaiva bhakti

  • Loving devotion to Shiva, often worshipped as the lingam.
  • Shiva is both fearsome ascetic and loving lord who chooses his devotees and saves them by grace.
  • The Nayanars' hymns (Tevaram) are still sung in Tamil Shiva temples; they shaped Shaiva Siddhanta theology.
  • Lingayats (Virashaivas), from Basava: each devotee wears a small lingam on the body, rejects temple priests and caste ranking, and worships Shiva directly.
  • Shaiva bhakti shows the same pattern as Vaishnava: local language, personal love, grace.
Mission 1

Yatra: pilgrimage as devotion

  • Yatra (pilgrimage): a journey to a holy place to receive darshan (sight) of the deity.
  • The saints themselves were pilgrims, singing at temple after temple.
  • Pandharpur wari: each year Varkari devotees walk about 250 km from Alandi and Dehu to Vithoba's temple, singing the hymns of Jnaneshvar and Tukaram, arriving for Ashadhi Ekadashi.
  • Vaishnava sites: Vrindavan and Mathura (Krishna), Ayodhya (Rama). Shaiva sites: Varanasi, the twelve jyotirlingas.
  • For the devotee, the hardship of the journey is itself an offering of love.
  • Darshan and the Ganges.
Mission 1Evaluate

Did bhakti make Hinduism open to all?

  • Claim: The bhakti movement made Hindu religious life open to everyone.
  • For: Gita 9:32 and the saints: women and low-caste devotees reach God directly.
  • For: Worship moved into local languages, homes, songs and pilgrim roads, needing no priest.
  • Against: Caste ranking survived; temples often stayed closed to Dalits until 20th-century laws and campaigns.
  • Against: Devotion was often made "inner": equal before God, but not equal in society.
  • Judgement criteria: Open spiritually or socially? Which region and century? Whose voices tell the story: saints, priests or later reformers?
Quick check
?Which belief is most central to bhakti, as taught by the bhakti saints?
Mission check

?At a mandir in Leicester, a young British Hindu sings Mirabai's songs to Krishna in Hindi, and a retired factory worker leads chants of Shiva's names. Neither is a priest or a Brahmin. Which feature of this scene comes most directly from the bhakti movement?

Bhakti carried devotion out of Sanskrit ritual into song, pilgrimage and the home. A later mission: puja and darshan.

Mission 2

Mission 2: In Hindu worship, why does seeing the deity matter, and being seen by it matter just as much?

Make a guess: In Hindu worship, why does seeing the deity matter, and being seen by it matter just as much?

Mission 2

What puja is

  • Puja: worship that honours a deity with offerings, as a beloved and honoured guest.
  • Offerings engage every sense: flowers, incense, a lamp, food, water, sandalwood paste, bells and song.
  • A short form has five offerings (panchopachara): scent, flower, incense, lamp, food. Fuller temple puja has sixteen (shodashopachara).
  • The worshipper often chants mantras and makes pranam (bowing, palms joined).
  • Aim: loving relationship with the deity (bhakti), and the deity's blessing.
  • For "the key aspects of puja", know: murti, offerings, arti, prasad, darshan.
Mission 2

Murti and darshan

  • A murti is a sacred image in which the deity is believed to be present, not an "idol" worshipped as mere stone or metal.
  • In a temple, a ceremony called prana pratishtha invites the deity's presence into the murti.
  • Darshan: "seeing". The devotee sees the deity and is seen by it; this exchange of sight is itself a blessing.
  • That is why the murti's eyes are prominent, and why curtains open for darshan at set times.
  • Scholar Diana Eck, Darśan: Seeing the Divine Image in India (1981), paraphrase: in Hindu worship, seeing is a way of touching and knowing the divine; darshan flows both ways.
Mission 2

Puja at home

  • Most Hindu homes have a shrine: a shelf, cabinet or small room, with murtis or pictures of the family's chosen deity (ishta-devata).
  • Daily: wash first; light a diya (lamp) and incense; offer flowers, water and food; ring a small bell; say mantras (e.g. the Gayatri mantra); perform a short arti.
  • Often led by women of the household; no priest needed.
  • Food cooked at home may be offered first, then eaten as blessed.
  • Personal and family: worship fits the rhythm of the day and the family's own tradition.
Mission 2

Puja in the mandir

  • A mandir is the home of the deity. Worshippers remove shoes, may ring the bell on entering, and approach the shrine.
  • The garbhagriha ("womb-house") holds the main murti, under the tower (shikhara); the hall (mandapa) is where people gather.
  • Pujaris (priests) care for the deity through the day: waking, bathing (abhisheka), dressing, offering food, arti, and putting to rest at night.
  • Worshippers bring offerings, receive darshan, join arti and bhajans (devotional songs).
  • Many British mandirs are also community centres: classes, weddings, meals, festivals.
Mission 2

Arti and prashad

  • Arti: a tray with a lamp of ghee wicks is waved in circles before the murti, with bells and a hymn (e.g. "Om Jai Jagdish Hare").
  • Worshippers pass their palms over the flame, then over their eyes and head: receiving the deity's light and blessing.
  • Prashad ("grace"): food offered to the deity is returned to the worshippers as blessed. Accepted with the right hand, and never thrown away.
  • Sharing prashad shares the deity's grace and binds the community.
  • Spelling: prasad.
Mission 2

Circumambulation

  • Pradakshina or parikrama: walking clockwise around the shrine or the murti, keeping the deity on one's right.
  • Meaning: the deity is the centre of life; the devotee's life revolves around God.
  • Done inside the temple's walkway around the garbhagriha, around sacred trees (the tulsi plant, the pipal) and around whole holy towns on pilgrimage.
  • Some devotees circle a set number of times, or prostrate at each step as a vow.
Quick check
?A visitor at a mandir says Hindus "worship statues". Which reply best explains what most Hindus believe about a murti?
Mission check

?A Hindu nurse in Birmingham cannot get to the mandir during a week of night shifts. Each morning she lights a diya before a small picture of Krishna, offers a flower and water, and draws the light over her eyes. Which statement best describes her worship?

The core of puja (offering, light, sight, blessing) is the same at a home shrine and a great temple. A later mission: pilgrimage and the Ganges.

Mission 3

Mission 3: Can a river wash away wrongdoing, and can a holy place exist outside India?

Make a guess: Can a river wash away wrongdoing, and can a holy place exist outside India?

Mission 3

Tirtha: a crossing place

  • A tirtha is a holy place. The word means a ford: a place to cross a river.
  • Hindus speak of tirthas as places where it is easier to cross over from this world towards the divine, and from samsara towards moksha (liberation).
  • Many tirthas are on rivers, coasts or mountains; many are linked to a story of a deity or a saint.
  • Yatra (or tirtha-yatra): a pilgrimage, a journey to a tirtha.
  • Pilgrims go for many reasons: to fulfil a vow, to ask for help, to give thanks, to remove the effects of wrongdoing, to perform rites for the dead, or simply for darshan.
Mission 3

Darshan: seeing and being seen

  • Darshan means seeing: the devotee sees the deity, and is seen by the deity.
  • At a shrine or mandir, the murti (sacred image) is not "just a statue": many Hindus believe the deity is present in it, especially after its consecration.
  • Darshan is a moment of blessing, not mainly an act of looking at art. Many murtis have large, open eyes for this reason.
  • Darshan can also be received from a holy person (a guru or saint) or from a sacred place: the river Ganges itself is "seen" as a goddess.
  • On pilgrimage, the long journey leads to darshan at the end: at a temple, a river or a mountain.
  • Darshan is one of the technical terms your spec says you must recognise.
Mission 3

Ganga Ma: the river as goddess

  • Hindus call the Ganges Ganga or Ganga Ma (Mother Ganga).
  • The story (told in the Ramayana and the Puranas, paraphrase): King Bhagiratha practised long austerities so that Ganga would come down from heaven to purify the ashes of his ancestors. Shiva caught her in his matted hair, so that her fall would not shatter the earth.
  • So the river is believed to flow from the divine world into this one: a tirtha along its whole length.
  • Bathing in Ganga is believed to purify: to wash away the effects of wrongdoing (papa).
  • Key places: Haridwar (where the river leaves the mountains), Prayagraj (meeting of Ganga, Yamuna and the unseen Sarasvati), Varanasi (Kashi, city of Shiva).
  • Kumbh Mela: a great bathing festival that rotates between Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik.
Mission 3

Death and the river

  • Water from the Ganges (Ganga jal) is kept in many Hindu homes, and a few drops may be placed in the mouth of a dying person.
  • Varanasi: many Hindus believe that to die in Kashi brings moksha, because Shiva himself whispers the words of liberation to the dying.
  • Cremation takes place on the ghats (riverside steps), e.g. Manikarnika Ghat.
  • After cremation, the ashes are immersed in the Ganges (asthi visarjan) if possible; families living elsewhere may carry or send the ashes to India.
  • Rites for ancestors (shraddha) are often performed at tirthas such as Gaya and Varanasi.
  • Not all Hindus share every belief: many see bathing as a symbol of inner purification, which still needs right action and devotion.
Quick check
?A pilgrim reaches a mandir at the end of a long yatra and stands before the murti of Krishna. What does she believe she receives in darshan?
Mission 3Read the source

Yatra as devotion

Krishna speaks in the Bhagavad Gita:

> "Whoso shall offer Me in faith and love / A leaf, a flower, a fruit, water poured forth, / That offering I accept, lovingly made / With pious will." (Bhagavad Gita 9:26, Arnold)

  • In bhakti (loving devotion) what matters is love, not the cost of the gift. A pilgrimage can be such an offering: a journey made for God.
  • Vaishnava example: the Pandharpur Wari in Maharashtra. Varkari devotees walk for weeks, singing, to Vithoba (a form of Vishnu/Krishna), carrying the sandals of the saints Jnaneshwar and Tukaram.
  • Shaiva example: the Kanwar Yatra. Devotees carry Ganga water from Haridwar and other places to pour over the linga of Shiva.

Q1 What does the verse suggest God values in an offering?

Show answer

The love and faith with which it is made, not its value.

Q2 Why might the Kanwar Yatra be called bhakti and not only ritual?

Show answer

The journey and the carried water are offered to Shiva in love.

Mission 3

Why India matters

  • Most tirthas are tied to stories set in India: Ayodhya (Rama), Mathura and Vrindavan (Krishna), Kurukshetra (the Gita), Varanasi (Shiva).
  • Many Hindus call India punya bhumi (holy land) or Bharat Mata (Mother India). The land itself, its rivers and mountains, is treated as sacred.
  • The Char Dham (four abodes: Badrinath, Dwarka, Puri, Rameswaram) mark the four corners of India: the whole land as one sacred circuit.
  • In the past, some orthodox Hindus believed crossing the ocean (kala pani, "black water") broke caste purity. Gandhi's caste group expelled him for sailing to England in 1888.
  • Hindus living elsewhere often keep links: pilgrimages to India, ashes taken to the Ganges, Ganga jal kept at home.
Mission 3Diversity

Sacred sites outside India

Old sites beyond modern India's borders:

  • Pashupatinath in Kathmandu, Nepal: a great Shiva temple.
  • Mount Kailash in Tibet: believed to be Shiva's abode; pilgrims walk round it.
  • Hinglaj in Pakistan: one of the Shakti Peethas (seats of the Goddess).

Newer sites, made by migrant communities:

  • Grand Bassin (Ganga Talao), Mauritius: a crater lake linked to the Ganges; pilgrims walk there at Maha Shivaratri.
  • Batu Caves, Malaysia: a Murugan shrine, focus of the Thaipusam festival.
  • UK: Skanda Vale in Wales; Bhaktivedanta Manor in Hertfordshire (ISKCON); the Neasden mandir in London.
  • How a site becomes sacred: a deity is installed in a murti by prana pratishtha (rite inviting the deity's presence); a saint lives there; a story or a "Ganga" is linked to it; pilgrims keep coming.
Mission 3Evaluate

Can a sacred site develop outside India?

  • Claim: A tirtha outside India can be as holy as one in India.
  • For: Brahman is everywhere; a consecrated murti makes the deity present anywhere.
  • For: Sacred geography has always moved: several Shakti Peethas lie outside modern India, and India has many "copies" of Kashi.
  • For: Grand Bassin and Skanda Vale already draw pilgrims as tirthas.
  • Against: The Ganges and the land of the epics cannot be moved; their holiness comes from where the gods acted.
  • Against: Many diaspora Hindus still take ashes to the Ganges and travel to India for pilgrimage.
  • Judgement criteria: What makes a place holy: the deity's presence, a story, the land itself, or the devotion of pilgrims? Do Hindus of different traditions answer differently?
Quick check
?A Hindu family in Britain asks why Grand Bassin in Mauritius is a pilgrimage site at all. Which answer explains this best?
Mission check

?Priya, a Hindu in Leicester, receives darshan every week at her local mandir, where the murtis were installed by prana pratishtha. She also asks her children to take her ashes to the Ganges after her death. What do her actions show?

For many Hindus, holiness is both everywhere and somewhere: God is present in every consecrated murti, yet some places, above all Ganga, carry a power of their own.

Mission 4

Mission 4: One law book says women must be honoured and also never independent. What do Hindus make of that?

Make a guess: One law book says women must be honoured and also never independent. What do Hindus make of that?

Mission 4

Stridharma: a woman's duty

  • Dharma is duty by one's place in life; stridharma is the dharma of women (stri, woman).
  • Classical texts set it mainly within the household: serving husband and family, keeping rituals of the home, raising children.
  • The ideal of the pativrata: a wife devoted to her husband, as Sita (Ramayana) and Savitri (Mahabharata) are remembered.
  • Texts were written by men, mostly Brahmin, for an ideal society; lived practice varied by region, jati and era.
  • Example: Tryambakayajvan's Stridharmapaddhati (18th century, Thanjavur), a rulebook for wives.
  • Many Hindu women also hold religious roles of their own: fasts (vratas) for family welfare, household puja, singing bhajans.
Mission 4Read the source

Two voices in the Manusmriti

Manusmriti 3.56 (paraphrase): where women are honoured, the gods rejoice; where they are not honoured, all rites bring no reward.

Manusmriti 5.147–148 and 9.3 (paraphrase): a woman should never act independently; she is protected by her father in childhood, her husband in youth and her sons in old age.

Q1 What do the two passages share?

Show answer

Both assume men are responsible for women: honour and protection.

Q2 Why can both feminists and traditionalists quote the Manusmriti?

Show answer

It both honours women and limits their independence.

  • The Manusmriti is smriti (remembered tradition), not shruti; many Hindus treat it as a product of its time.
Mission 4

Marriage at the centre

  • Vivaha (marriage) is one of the samskaras (life-cycle rites) and opens the grihastha (householder) stage.
  • Traditionally a sacred, lifelong bond, not a contract: the couple take seven steps (saptapadi) around the sacred fire.
  • Kanyadan: the father gives his daughter in marriage; she joins her husband's family.
  • For women, classical texts treat marriage as their main samskara, in place of the student initiation boys receive.
  • Children: the householder's duty includes continuing the family and its rites.
  • Many Hindu marriages are arranged (by families, with the couple's consent); "love marriages" are increasingly common.
Mission 4

Brahmacharya and celibacy

  • Brahmacharya: (1) the student stage of life; (2) celibacy and self-control in general.
  • The student stage, with the sacred-thread initiation (upanayana), was traditionally for boys of the three upper varnas.
  • Yet the Upanishads name women thinkers: Gargi and Maitreyi debate and question in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (3.6, 3.8; 2.4).
  • Atharva Veda 11.5.18 links a girl's brahmacharya to finding a good husband (paraphrase): some read this as evidence of early education for girls.
  • Celibacy is honoured in sannyasa (renunciation) and by many gurus; Gandhi took a vow of brahmacharya in 1906.
  • Women renunciants today: e.g. Sri Sarada Math (founded 1954), led by women monks.
  • Most Hindus see marriage, not celibacy, as the normal path; celibacy is a calling for some, or for later life.
Mission 4

Divorce: different views

  • Traditional view (classical dharmashastras): marriage is indissoluble, for this life and beyond; a widow does not remarry.
  • But texts disagree: Narada Smriti 12.97 (paraphrase) lets a woman take another husband if hers is lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or is outcaste.
  • Many jatis always allowed separation and remarriage by local custom.
  • Hindu Marriage Act 1955: divorce on set grounds; divorce by mutual consent added in 1976.
  • Many Hindus today accept divorce as a lesser evil than a harmful marriage; others see it as against dharma and seek reconciliation through families.
  • Divorce still carries stigma, often heavier for women.
Mission 4

Same-sex relationships and transgender matters

  • No single Hindu view, and no central authority.
  • Third nature (tritiya prakriti): the Kama Sutra (c. 3rd century CE) describes people of a "third nature".
  • Gender in sacred stories: Ardhanarishvara (Shiva and Parvati as one half-male, half-female form); Mohini (Vishnu's female form); Shikhandi (Mahabharata), born female and later male.
  • Hijra communities (often trans women) have a recognised ritual role at births and weddings; they honour the goddess Bahuchara Mata.
  • Conservative views: the dharma texts set penances for same-sex acts; marriage is for children; ISKCON teaches sex only in marriage for procreation.
  • Accepting views: some Hindus and Hindu LGBT groups see diversity of nature within dharma; atman has no gender.
  • Indian law: third gender recognised (Supreme Court, NALSA, 2014); same-sex acts decriminalised (Navtej Singh Johar, 2018); no same-sex marriage (Supreme Court, 2023).
  • Skill tip (AO1): show diversity: name the group or source each view comes from.
Quick check

Quick check

Mission 4

Changing roles of men and women

  • Education and work: Hindu women now work in every profession; many families value daughters' education as highly as sons'.
  • Religious roles: women priests (pujaris) trained in some places (e.g. by the Shankar Seva Samiti and Jnana Prabodhini in Pune); women gurus (e.g. Anandamayi Ma, 1896–1982; Mata Amritanandamayi, b. 1953).
  • Roles of men: more shared housework and child care in many families; but the provider role and son preference persist.
  • Diaspora: British Hindu women lead temple committees and teach in Hindu schools.
  • Many Hindus reinterpret stridharma as mutual duties of partners; traditionalists see the old roles as complementary, not unequal.
Mission check

?Priya, a British Hindu surgeon, keeps a weekly vrata for her family and says: "Stridharma for me means caring duties shared with my husband, not obeying him." How is her view best described?

Hindu teaching on women speaks in more than one voice, and Hindus today choose and reinterpret between those voices. Next: how reformers and feminists changed women's lives.

Mission 5

Mission 5: Sati was banned in 1829. Did change for Hindu women come from inside the tradition or outside?

Make a guess: Sati was banned in 1829. Did change for Hindu women come from inside the tradition or outside?

Mission 5

An encounter with empire

  • From the late 1700s, Britain ruled more and more of India: new laws, missionary schools, Western ideas of rights and reason.
  • Missionaries and officials often attacked Hindu practice, especially the treatment of women.
  • Hindu reformers answered in two ways at once: they used Western arguments and went back to Hindu texts to show that harmful customs were not true dharma.
  • Later, India's secular state (from 1947) gave women rights by law, outside religion.
  • So change came from three sources: reformers within, colonial rule, and the secular state. How much from each is debated.
Mission 5

Sati

  • Sati: a widow burning herself, or being burned, on her husband's funeral pyre. Named after the goddess Sati, though in her story she was not a widow.
  • Never universal: practised mainly among some higher castes in some regions; cases rose in early 19th-century Bengal.
  • Defenders praised it as the supreme act of a pativrata (devoted wife); opponents called it murder, often under family pressure.
  • Banned in Bengal in 1829 (Governor-General William Bentinck), after Hindu reformers' campaigns. Ram Mohan Roy (1772–1833) argued from Hindu law books that sati was not required.
  • A case in Rajasthan in 1987 (Roop Kanwar) led to the Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act 1987, which also bans glorifying sati.
Mission 5

Ram Mohan Roy

  • Ram Mohan Roy (1772–1833), Bengali scholar of Sanskrit, Persian and English; founded the Brahmo Sabha (1828), later the Brahmo Samaj.
  • Campaigned against sati in tracts (1818, 1820) and petitions; supported the 1829 ban and defended it in England before the Privy Council; he died in Bristol in 1833.
  • His method: argue from the shastras. The texts do not command sati; they praise a widow's chaste, disciplined life (paraphrase).
  • Also argued for women's property rights (1822), against polygamy, and for women's education.
  • Significance: he made the case for women's rights as a Hindu, from inside the tradition.
Mission 5Read the source

Roy's appeal to Manu

Manusmriti 5.157–160 (paraphrase): after her husband's death a widow should live a pure, self-controlled life; a virtuous wife who remains chaste after his death reaches heaven, even without a son.

  • Roy cited verses like these: Manu, the highest authority among the law books, praises a widow who lives, not one who dies.
  • Opponents cited other texts (later smritis and Puranas) that praised sati.

Q1 How could this passage be used against sati?

Show answer

It praises a widow's life of discipline, with heaven as its reward, not death on the pyre.

Q2 What does Roy's method show about reform in Hinduism?

Show answer

Reform can work by choosing which texts are authoritative and how to read them.

Mission 5

Widows, daughters, education

  • Widows faced shaved heads, white clothes, poverty and a ban on remarriage in many high-caste families.
  • Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (1820–1891) argued from the Parashara Smriti for widow remarriage: Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act 1856.
  • Education: Savitribai Phule (1831–1897) opened a girls' school in Pune (1848) with Jyotirao Phule; the Arya Samaj founded girls' schools; Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922) opened a home for widows (1889).
  • Child marriage was restricted by the Child Marriage Restraint Act (1929).
  • Daughters: rights to inherit came later.
Quick check
?How did Ram Mohan Roy mainly argue against sati?
Mission 5

Rights from a secular state

  • The Constitution (1950): equality before the law (Article 14), no discrimination by sex (Article 15); every adult woman can vote.
  • The Hindu Code (1955–56): Hindu Marriage Act (monogamy, divorce); Hindu Succession Act (daughters inherit); adoption and guardianship laws. Ambedkar resigned as Law Minister in 1951 partly because the bill was delayed.
  • 2005: daughters gain equal rights in ancestral family property.
  • Laws on dowry (1961), sex selection (1994), domestic violence (2005).
  • Outside religion: education, jobs and cities changed roles of men and women; many men now share work once called women's.
  • Some Hindus welcomed this as true dharma; others saw state interference in religious law.
Mission 5

Manushi and Madhu Kishwar

  • Manushi: founded in Delhi in 1978 by Madhu Kishwar (b. 1951) and Ruth Vanita; a journal "about women and society".
  • Work: reporting violence against women, dowry deaths and unfair laws; campaigns for women's land and property rights; giving ordinary women space to speak.
  • Later, as Manushi Sangathan, it also campaigned for poor workers such as Delhi's street vendors.
  • Kishwar's essay "Why I do not call myself a feminist" (1990): Western feminist labels may not fit Indian women's lives (paraphrase).
  • She drew on Indian culture as a resource, e.g. reading Sita as a woman of moral strength who challenged Rama's injustice (1997).
  • Significance: feminism with Indian and Hindu resources, not only against them.
Mission 5Evaluate

Is feminism an issue in Hinduism today?

  • Claim: Feminism is still a live issue in Hinduism today.
  • For: dowry, son preference and widow stigma persist; some texts limit women's independence.
  • For: Dalit feminists show women are still unequal within caste.
  • Against: law gives equal rights; many Hindu women lead, teach and serve as priests.
  • Against: Kishwar and others say Hindu culture gives women resources, so a Western-style feminism is not needed.
  • Judgement criteria: issue in teaching, or in culture? Which women: urban or rural, upper-caste or Dalit? Measured by law or by daily life?
Quick check
?Which statement best describes Madhu Kishwar's approach?
Mission 5

Change from inside or outside?

  • Inside: Roy argued from the shastras; bhakti saints gave women voice.
  • Vidyasagar argued from the Parashara Smriti for widow remarriage.
  • Kishwar drew on Sita as a woman of moral strength.
  • Outside: British law (1829 sati ban; 1856 widow remarriage), the secular Constitution and Hindu Code, economic change.
  • Both: most reforms needed Hindu arguments and state law.
  • Impact on men: new laws changed fathers' and husbands' duties (shared property, no dowry, divorce), and many men's roles at home.
Mission check

?A Hindu temple trust in Britain votes to let women lead the main arti. Supporters cite women saints and the Manusmriti's teaching that where women are honoured, the gods rejoice. Which kind of reform is this most like?

Change for Hindu women came from reformers reading their own texts, from colonial and secular law, and from women's own voices. Next: Hindu teaching on wealth and poverty.

Mission 6

Mission 6: Ancient hymns, ancient astronomers, a universe billions of years old: does science fit Hindu belief?

Make a guess: Ancient hymns, ancient astronomers, a universe billions of years old: does science fit Hindu belief?

Mission 6

Why science is a test for any religion

  • Modern science asks for evidence and reason: claims are tested, and can be revised.
  • Religions often rest on revelation (for Hindus, shruti, "what is heard": the Vedas) and on tradition.
  • So science can challenge a tradition in three ways:
  • Method: is faith reasonable without evidence?
  • Discoveries: an old universe (Big Bang), evolution (Darwin).
  • Ethics: new powers (genetic engineering) raise new moral questions.
  • Hindus have answered in very different ways, from "no conflict at all" to firm rejection of parts of science.
Mission 6

Science inside the tradition

  • Many Hindus point out that Indian thinkers did science long before modern Europe.
  • Astronomy: Aryabhata (476–c. 550 CE), Aryabhatiya (499 CE): the earth turns on its axis; a value of π close to 3.1416; explained eclipses by shadows.
  • Brahmagupta (598–c. 668 CE): rules for calculating with zero and negative numbers.
  • Medicine: Ayurveda ("knowledge of long life"). The Charaka Samhita (internal medicine) and the Sushruta Samhita (surgery), compiled in the centuries around the turn of the era.
  • Astronomy grew partly from religious need: jyotisha set the right times for Vedic rituals.
Mission 6

Samkhya: classifying matter

  • Samkhya ("enumeration") is one of the six classical schools (darshanas); its key text is the Samkhya Karika (c. 4th–5th century CE).
  • Two ultimate realities: purusha (pure consciousness) and prakriti (matter, nature).
  • Prakriti is made of three gunas: sattva (clarity), rajas (energy), tamas (inertia).
  • It unfolds into twenty-four principles (tattvas), ending in the five gross elements: space, air, fire, water, earth.
  • Some Hindus see this as an early, reasoned classification of matter: an ancestor of science.
  • Others note it is a philosophy of liberation, not experiment: it classifies matter to free purusha from it.
Mission 6

"It was all in the Vedas"

  • Some Hindus hold that modern discoveries were revealed in the Vedas long ago.
  • Dayananda Saraswati (1824–1883), founder of the Arya Samaj, Satyarth Prakash (1875): the Vedas are the source of all true knowledge, including science (paraphrase).
  • Popular claims today: flying machines (vimanas) in the epics; nuclear weapons; "Vedic mathematics".
  • Critics, including many Hindu scientists and historians: these readings put modern ideas back into ancient texts; they can make Indian science look like myth and hide its real achievements.
  • Supporters: the Vedas are eternal knowledge, so modern science rediscovers what the rishis saw.
Mission 6

Radhakrishnan: a scientific religion

  • Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan (1888–1975), philosopher; President of India 1962–1967. The Hindu View of Life (1927); An Idealist View of Life (1932).
  • His claim (paraphrase): Hinduism rests on experience, not dogma. The rishis were explorers who tested their insight in meditation, as scientists test theories.
  • Religious truth is reached by intuition (anubhava, direct experience), checked by reason and by others' experience.
  • Hinduism is open: it can absorb new knowledge without crisis, because it has no fixed creed.
  • So science and Hinduism are compatible: both seek the truth about one reality.
  • Critics: religious experience cannot be repeated and checked as a lab result can; and his "Hinduism" is mostly Advaita Vedanta, not the whole tradition.
Mission 6Read the source

Days and nights of Brahma

Bhagavad Gita 8.18 (Edwin Arnold, 1885):

> "When that vast Dawn doth break, th' Invisible / Is brought anew into the Visible; / When that deep Night doth darken, all which is / Fades back again to Him Who sent it forth"

  • Hindu cosmology is cyclical: universes emerge and dissolve again and again.
  • A kalpa (a "day of Brahma") is usually reckoned at 4.32 billion years.
  • Many Hindus say the Big Bang fits: it can be the dawn of the present cycle, and the vast scale of time matches modern cosmology.

Q1 According to the passage, where does everything go at "Night"?

Show answer

Back into the one who sent it forth: the unmanifest source.

Q2 Name one difference between this picture and a single Big Bang.

Show answer

Cycles without first beginning, against one beginning about 13.8 billion years ago.

Quick check
?Which belief best describes Radhakrishnan's case that Hinduism is compatible with science?
Mission 6

Darwin: three Hindu responses

  • Acceptance: many Hindus accept evolution. There was no Hindu "Genesis" debate: no fixed six-day creation to defend.
  • Avatar reading: some see a parallel in the ten avatars of Vishnu (fish → tortoise → boar → man-lion → dwarf → human forms). Critics: the avatars are divine descents, not species changing over time.
  • Spiritual evolution: Sri Aurobindo (1872–1950), The Life Divine (1939–40): evolution is real, but it is spirit unfolding in matter towards higher consciousness.
  • Hindus differ on natural selection: acceptance of common descent is wider than acceptance that blind chance explains everything.
  • A soul (atman) passes through many bodies (samsara); for many Hindus that is about the self, not about biology.
Mission 6

ISKCON: devolution, not evolution

  • ISKCON (International Society for Krishna Consciousness), founded 1966 by A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada (1896–1977).
  • Prabhupada rejected Darwinian evolution: life comes from life, and consciousness cannot come from matter.
  • Species are bodies through which souls move by karma: traditionally 8,400,000 forms of life (from the Puranas).
  • The Bhaktivedanta Institute (founded 1976) argues against materialist science. Michael Cremo and Richard Thompson, Forbidden Archeology (1993), argue humans are far older than evolution allows.
  • Cremo's Human Devolution (2003): souls descend from a spiritual world into matter.
  • Most scientists reject these claims; ISKCON sees them as defending the Vedas' account against materialism.
  • Big Bang: ISKCON reads creation as Krishna's cyclical creation through Maha-Vishnu, not a chance event.
Quick check
?Which view would most ISKCON teachers hold about the origin of human beings?
Mission 6

Genetic engineering

  • Science as a stimulus to ethics: new powers force new moral thinking.
  • For (many Hindus): healing is dharma; Ayurveda honours the physician; compassion (daya) supports gene therapy to end suffering.
  • Ahimsa (non-harm) cuts both ways: curing disease prevents harm, but research may destroy embryos; many Hindus hold that the atman is present from conception.
  • Karma: some ask whether removing a genetic condition interferes with karma; others reply that a doctor's help can itself be part of one's karma.
  • Sex selection and "designer babies": strong concern in India, where sex-selective abortion is banned (Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act 1994).
  • GM crops: debated in India (e.g. Bt cotton). Critics draw on reverence for nature and farmers' seed; supporters stress feeding people.
  • No single Hindu authority decides: views vary by tradition, guru and individual conscience.
  • Skill tip (AO1): give two different Hindu responses, each linked to a named principle (ahimsa, karma, dharma).
Mission 6Evaluate

How effective are Hindu responses to science?

  • Claim: Hinduism has met the challenge of science more easily than other religions.
  • For: no fixed creation date; cyclical vast time fits cosmology; experience-based religion (Radhakrishnan) can absorb new knowledge.
  • For: a real history of Indian science (Aryabhata, Ayurveda) gives Hindus pride, not suspicion, towards science.
  • Against: "It was all in the Vedas" claims may avoid the challenge rather than meet it.
  • Against: ISKCON and others reject evolution: there is real conflict for some Hindus.
  • Against: easy fit may come from making Hinduism vague: if anything fits, does belief say anything?
  • Judgement criteria: Which Hindus? (conservative and liberal differ.) Fit with science, or fit with the tradition? Does the response face evidence fairly?
Mission check

?A Hindu doctor says: "Ayurveda and modern medicine are both ways of knowing the body. I use what the evidence supports, and I see my healing work as my dharma." Which response to science is closest to hers?

Hindu responses to science run from "no conflict at all" to firm rejection of parts of science, with claims that it was all in the Vedas in between. Next: how Hindu teaching meets caste and equality.

Mission 7

Mission 7: How did one elderly monk with almost no money spread Krishna devotion across the world?

Make a guess: How did one elderly monk with almost no money spread Krishna devotion across the world?

Mission 7

Roots: Chaitanya and Gaudiya Vaishnavism

  • ISKCON: the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, founded in New York in 1966. Popularly "the Hare Krishnas".
  • It belongs to Gaudiya Vaishnavism, the Bengal ("Gauda") devotional tradition.
  • Founder of that tradition: Chaitanya Mahaprabhu (1486–1534), who led ecstatic group chanting of Krishna's names (sankirtan) in the streets.
  • Key texts: the Bhagavad Gita and the Bhagavata Purana (Srimad Bhagavatam).
  • ISKCON sees itself as part of an unbroken chain of teachers (parampara) back to Chaitanya and Krishna.
Mission 7

Krishna consciousness

  • Krishna consciousness: every soul's original nature is to love and serve Krishna. We forget this and identify with the body.
  • The soul (jiva) is eternal, both one with Krishna in quality and different from him: achintya-bhedabheda ("inconceivable oneness and difference", Chaitanya's teaching).
  • So ISKCON rejects Advaita's impersonal Brahman as the highest truth: God is a person.
  • Goal: pure loving devotion (prema bhakti) and return to Krishna's eternal realm, not merging into Brahman.
  • In this age of quarrel (Kali Yuga) the easiest path is chanting God's names.
  • The maha-mantra: "Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare / Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare".
Quick check
?Why does ISKCON reject the Advaita Vedanta goal of merging into Brahman?
Mission 7

A regulated life

  • Four regulative principles for initiated devotees:
  • no meat, fish or eggs · no intoxicants (including alcohol, tobacco, tea and coffee) · no gambling · no sex outside marriage.
  • Chant 16 rounds of the maha-mantra a day on 108-bead japa mala.
  • Temple day begins about 4:30 am with mangala arati; worship of the deities Radha and Krishna.
  • Food cooked for Krishna and shared as prasadam; free meals (Food for Life).
  • Public chanting (harinama), book distribution, festivals such as Rathayatra (chariot procession, London since 1969).
Mission 7

Why did it grow?

Religious reasons

  • A clear, personal God and a simple daily practice (chanting) open to anyone.
  • An authority: an ancient lineage, a guru, and English translations with commentary.

Cultural reasons

  • 1960s counterculture: young Westerners looking beyond materialism and drugs; communal living.
  • Celebrity: George Harrison produced the "Hare Krishna Mantra" single (1969) and gave Bhaktivedanta Manor (Hertfordshire, 1973).
  • Diaspora: from the 1970s, Indian Hindus in Britain and America joined temples in large numbers: Vaishnava worship they knew, explained in English to their children.
  • In secular Britain it offered what secularisation had removed: community, moral rules and a source of truth.
Quick check
?Which of these is one of ISKCON's four regulative principles for initiated devotees?
Mission 7

ISKCON and science

  • Darwin: Prabhupada rejected the view that life and humans arose by unguided natural selection.
  • ISKCON's alternative: the soul passes through 8,400,000 species of body (from the Puranas); "evolution" is the soul's journey, not the body's.
  • The Bhaktivedanta Institute (founded 1974) argued for consciousness as prior to matter; Forbidden Archeology (Cremo and Thompson, 1993) claimed humans have existed for millions of years.
  • Big Bang: universes come from and return to God in vast cycles (Bhagavata cosmology); ISKCON rejects a universe that begins by chance, not the idea of a beginning as such.
  • Most scientists reject these claims; other Hindus (e.g. Radhakrishnan, see Mission 6) welcome evolution.
Mission 7Evaluate

"ISKCON is a divergence from traditional Hinduism."

  • For divergence: converts from outside Indian birth and caste; it seeks converts, unlike most Hindu traditions; one God (Krishna) is supreme and other deities are servants of Krishna; strict rules most Hindus do not follow; a global, centrally governed organisation; it has sometimes avoided the word "Hindu".
  • Against: its theology is 500 years old (Chaitanya); its texts are classic Hindu scriptures; Gaudiya temples in India recognise it; most of its members in Britain are Hindus of Indian origin; Hindu bodies in Britain treat it as Hindu.
  • Deeper question: is there one "traditional" Hinduism to diverge from? (.)
  • Judge it by: beliefs, practice, membership, organisation: which matters most for "traditional"?
Mission check

?A British Gujarati family who have always worshipped Krishna at home begin attending an ISKCON temple. Which feature of ISKCON is most likely to be new to them?

ISKCON's beliefs are old Gaudiya Vaishnavism; what was new was its global mission, its converts and its organisation.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • Bhakti is loving devotion to a personal God; liberation comes by grace and surrender.
  • It began with the Tamil Alvars (Vishnu) and Nayanars (Shiva), c. 6th–9th centuries, and spread north through saints of every caste, singing in local languages.

Mission 2

  • Puja honours a deity with offerings to the senses; darshan is the two-way sight between devotee and deity, believed present in the murti.
  • In the mandir: garbhagriha, pujaris, arti, prashad and clockwise circumambulation; at home: a family shrine, often led by women.

Mission 3

  • A tirtha is a "crossing place"; on yatra, pilgrims seek darshan (seeing and being seen by the deity), purification and help for the dead.
  • Ganga is a goddess believed to have come down from heaven; bathing purifies, and ashes are immersed in her waters.
  • India matters as the land of the gods' stories, but tirthas can develop elsewhere (Grand Bassin, Skanda Vale); Hindus weigh this differently.

Mission 4

  • Stridharma sets women's duty within the household; the Manusmriti both honours women and limits their independence.
  • Hindus hold different views on celibacy (brahmacharya).
  • Hindus hold different views on divorce, from indissoluble marriage to divorce as a lesser evil.
  • Hindus hold different views on same-sex relationships and gender identity.

Mission 5

  • Under British rule, reformers such as Ram Mohan Roy argued from the shastras against sati and for women's rights; laws followed (1829 sati ban; 1856 widow remarriage).
  • The secular state and the Hindu Code gave women legal rights; Manushi and Madhu Kishwar sought women's rights with Indian cultural resources.

Mission 6

  • Science tests religion by its method, its discoveries and its new ethical powers; Hindus respond in many ways.
  • Compatibility (Radhakrishnan; cyclical cosmology and the Big Bang), revelation claims (science "in the Vedas") and rejection (ISKCON's devolution against Darwin) are three distinct responses.
  • Genetic engineering is weighed through ahimsa, karma, dharma and compassion, with no single Hindu verdict.

Mission 7

  • ISKCON (1966) brings Chaitanya's Gaudiya Vaishnava bhakti to the world: Krishna is the supreme person; chant his names.
  • Practice: four regulative principles, 16 rounds of japa, temple worship, prasadam; growth came from Prabhupada, the counterculture and the Indian diaspora.
  • ISKCON rejects Darwinian evolution and a chance-born universe; other Hindus respond differently (see Mission 6).
